p: We planted a bean seed in a cup. We gave it water and put it by the window. After a week, a little green shoot came up.
The moon goes around the Earth. Sometimes it looks round and sometimes it looks thin. We can see it best at night.

s: The Earth takes about three hundred and sixty-five days to orbit the sun.
Plants make their own food using sunlight in a process called photosynthesis.
Gravity is the force that pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth.
The Parkes radio telescope helped broadcast the first moon landing in 1969.
Sound travels as vibrations through air, water and solid objects.
Saturn's rings are made of billions of pieces of ice and rock.
A fair test changes only one variable at a time.
Solids, liquids and gases are the three common states of matter.
Electric circuits need a complete loop for the current to flow.
Fossils show us what animals and plants lived millions of years ago.
The water cycle includes evaporation, condensation and precipitation.
Friction slows things down when two surfaces rub together.
The International Space Station orbits the Earth about every ninety minutes.
Our skeleton protects our organs and helps us move.
We tested which paper towel could absorb the most water.
Day and night happen because the Earth spins on its axis.
Venus is the hottest planet even though Mercury is closer to the sun.
Scientists record their observations carefully in a notebook.
Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity.
A food chain shows what eats what in an ecosystem.
Rust forms when iron reacts with water and oxygen.
Light travels faster than anything else in the universe.
The Southern Cross is a group of stars seen from Australia.
Insects have six legs and three main body parts.
Engineers test their designs and improve them after each trial.
p: The water cycle moves water around our planet. The sun heats water in oceans and lakes, and it evaporates into the air. As the water vapour rises and cools, it forms clouds. When the droplets get heavy, they fall as rain, filling rivers that flow back to the sea.

Our class investigated how the length of a ramp affects how far a toy car travels. We kept the car, the surface and the starting point the same. We only changed the height of the ramp. The higher the ramp, the further the car rolled.

The Parkes telescope in New South Wales is a giant radio dish. In 1969 it received television pictures of astronauts walking on the moon. Millions of people around the world watched those pictures. Today the telescope still helps scientists study distant stars and galaxies.

Plants are amazing because they make their own food. Their leaves capture sunlight and use it to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar. This process is called photosynthesis. It also releases oxygen into the air, which people and animals need to breathe.

Magnets have two ends called the north pole and the south pole. If you put two north poles together, they push each other away. If you put a north pole near a south pole, they pull together. Magnets are used in fridges, speakers and electric motors.

Fossils are the remains or traces of living things from long ago. They form when a plant or animal is buried in mud or sand that slowly turns to rock. Australia has many important fossil sites, including places where dinosaur footprints can still be seen.

s: The scientific method involves asking a question, forming a hypothesis, testing it and analysing the results.
Cells are the basic building blocks of all living things, from bacteria to blue whales.
Australian scientists invented the black box flight recorder, which helps investigators understand plane crashes.
Elements are listed on the periodic table according to the number of protons in their atoms.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year, nearly ten trillion kilometres.
Vaccines train the immune system to recognise and fight specific diseases.
Renewable energy sources, such as wind and solar, produce electricity without burning fossil fuels.
Chemical reactions can release energy as heat and light, as seen in a burning candle.
The theory of plate tectonics explains how continents slowly move across the Earth's surface.
DNA carries the genetic instructions that determine many of an organism's characteristics.
Newton's first law states that an object stays still or keeps moving unless a force acts on it.
Telescopes in remote deserts avoid the light pollution that makes stars hard to see from cities.
Australian researchers developed the technology behind fast wireless internet connections.
Acids and bases can be identified using indicators that change colour.
Biodiversity describes the variety of life found in a particular habitat or on the planet as a whole.
Penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic, was developed with the help of Australian scientist Howard Florey.
The moon's gravity causes the tides that rise and fall along our coastlines.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form into another.
Space probes have travelled beyond the planets to the edge of our solar system.
A controlled experiment compares a test group with a control group that receives no treatment.
Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving.
Microscopes revealed a world of tiny organisms invisible to the naked eye.
Earthquakes occur when stress builds up along faults and is suddenly released.
Indigenous astronomy uses the stars to mark seasons and guide travel across the land.
Peer review allows other experts to check a study before it is published.
p: The scientific method is a process that helps scientists investigate questions about the world. It begins with an observation that leads to a question. The scientist then forms a hypothesis, a possible explanation that can be tested. Experiments are designed to test the hypothesis, and the results are analysed. If the results do not support the hypothesis, it is revised and tested again.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have studied the night sky for tens of thousands of years. One well-known example is the Emu in the Sky, a shape formed by dark dust clouds in the Milky Way. Its position at different times of year signalled when emus were laying eggs. This shows how astronomy was closely linked to seasonal knowledge and survival.

Vaccines have saved millions of lives by preventing diseases such as polio, measles and whooping cough. A vaccine contains a weakened or harmless part of a germ, or instructions to make one. This trains the immune system to recognise the real germ quickly if a person is exposed later. When most people in a community are vaccinated, it also protects those who cannot be.

The Earth's outer layer is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. These plates move very slowly, only a few centimetres each year. Where plates collide, mountains can form, and where they pull apart, new crust is created. Australia sits in the middle of a plate, which is why it experiences fewer major earthquakes and volcanoes than countries such as New Zealand.

Renewable energy is growing rapidly in Australia. Rooftop solar panels are now found on millions of homes, and large wind farms generate electricity in many regions. Because the sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow, energy storage is important. Large batteries and pumped hydro schemes store extra energy so it can be used when demand is high.

The microscope transformed our understanding of life. Before it was invented, people had no idea that tiny organisms lived in water, soil and even inside their own bodies. Scientists such as Antonie van Leeuwenhoek observed bacteria for the first time in the seventeenth century. Today, powerful electron microscopes can show details as small as individual molecules.

s: The scientific consensus on climate change rests on multiple independent lines of evidence gathered over many decades.
Quantum computing exploits principles such as superposition to perform certain calculations far faster than classical computers.
CRISPR gene editing allows scientists to modify DNA with unprecedented precision, raising important ethical questions.
The Square Kilometre Array, partly built in Western Australia, will be one of the most powerful radio telescopes ever constructed.
Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria evolve to survive drugs that once killed them.
Peer review is an imperfect but essential mechanism for maintaining the quality of published research.
Dark matter cannot be observed directly, yet its gravitational effects shape the structure of galaxies.
Australian researchers developed the cervical cancer vaccine, which has prevented countless infections worldwide.
Correlation does not prove causation, a principle that is frequently ignored in media reports of scientific studies.
Nuclear fusion promises abundant clean energy, but sustaining the necessary conditions remains extraordinarily difficult.
The reproducibility crisis has prompted scientists to share data and methods more openly.
Gravitational waves, predicted by Einstein, were finally detected a century after he proposed them.
Synthetic biology combines engineering and biology to design organisms that perform useful tasks.
Funding decisions inevitably shape which scientific questions are investigated and which are neglected.
Machine learning models can identify patterns in medical images that even experienced specialists may miss.
The discovery of exoplanets has transformed our estimates of how common Earth-like worlds may be.
Science communication plays a crucial role in building public trust and countering misinformation.
Ethical guidelines govern research involving human participants to protect their safety, privacy and consent.
Australian scientists have played leading roles in developing solar cell technology used around the world.
Emergent properties arise when complex systems behave in ways that cannot be predicted from their individual parts.
Interdisciplinary research increasingly drives breakthroughs at the boundaries between traditional fields.
The precautionary principle suggests caution when an action may cause serious harm, even without complete certainty.
Particle accelerators collide atoms at enormous speeds to reveal the fundamental building blocks of matter.
Indigenous knowledge systems offer insights into ecology and astronomy that complement Western science.
Scientific literacy enables citizens to evaluate evidence and participate meaningfully in public debates.
p: Antibiotic resistance is considered one of the greatest threats to global health. When antibiotics are overused or used incorrectly, bacteria that survive can pass on their resistance, eventually producing strains that no available drug can treat. Routine surgeries and minor infections could once again become dangerous. Addressing this problem requires more careful prescribing, reduced use of antibiotics in agriculture and renewed investment in developing new drugs, an area many pharmaceutical companies have found unprofitable.

Gene editing technologies such as CRISPR have made it possible to alter specific sections of DNA quickly and cheaply. Researchers hope these tools could cure inherited diseases, create crops that withstand drought and even control invasive pests. However, editing human embryos raises profound ethical concerns, because changes would be passed to future generations. Many scientists have called for strict international regulation to ensure the technology is used responsibly and with broad public consent.

Australia's southern skies and remote locations make it an ideal place for astronomy. The Square Kilometre Array, being built in Western Australia and South Africa, will link thousands of antennas to study the early universe, the formation of galaxies and the nature of dark energy. Its sensitivity depends on radio quiet zones where mobile phones and other transmitters are restricted. The project demonstrates how international collaboration can tackle questions no single nation could answer alone.

The reproducibility crisis refers to the discovery that many published scientific findings cannot be replicated when other researchers repeat the experiments. Contributing factors include small sample sizes, pressure to publish surprising results and flexible analysis methods that make chance findings appear significant. In response, journals and funding bodies are encouraging pre-registration of studies, open data and the publication of negative results. These reforms aim to strengthen the reliability of science without discouraging innovation.

Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research. Machine learning systems have predicted the three-dimensional structures of proteins, a problem that challenged biologists for decades, and are helping astronomers sift through vast quantities of telescope data. Yet these tools also introduce risks. Models trained on biased data can produce misleading results, and their internal reasoning is often difficult to interpret. Scientists must therefore combine computational power with careful human judgement and validation.

Scientific knowledge is always provisional, meaning it can be revised when new evidence emerges. This is a strength rather than a weakness, yet it is sometimes misunderstood by the public, who may see changing advice as a sign of confusion. Effective science communication explains not only what scientists know, but also how they know it and how confident they are. Building this understanding helps communities make informed decisions about health, technology and the environment.
